title: How to Set Up a Home Security Camera System for Under $200
excerpt: Two cameras, smart placement, and memory-card storage: how to cover your front door and key rooms on a tight budget with a one-weekend plan.
body:
A two-hundred-dollar budget buys a genuinely useful camera system if you spend it on coverage rather than cameras. Most people do the opposite: they buy one feature-loaded camera, point it at the driveway, and leave the front door unwatched. A cheaper pair of cameras covering the two places a stranger must pass through records more usable evidence than any single premium unit watching one angle.

The plan below splits that budget across two plug-in cameras, local storage, and mounts, then installs everything in a single weekend. All you need is outlets and Wi-Fi at both spots.

What a tight budget actually covers: two cameras and a plan

Divide the budget into three slices. The largest goes to two plug-in Wi-Fi cameras with at least 1080p resolution, sharp enough to recognize a face at doorway distance. The next goes to a memory card for each camera, so clips stay in your home instead of behind a subscription. The smallest covers mounts and cord routing. A shopping list with no room left for storage and mounting is not a system yet, just two cameras in boxes.

Accept what the budget cannot do: two cameras will not cover every window, the backyard, and the garage at once. Each decision below puts those two lenses where strangers have no choice but to walk past them. Our roundup of budget-friendly camera options helps once you know which two spots you are filling.

Cover the front door first, then one indoor choke point

Camera one watches the approach to the front door: a window sill, an indoor shelf near the entry, or a sheltered porch mount. The goal is a clear view of every visitor's face plus packages on the step. Check the view at night before committing, because glass reflections can turn a perfect daytime angle into a useless mirror after dark.

Camera two watches the indoor choke point every intruder must cross, usually the hallway to the bedrooms or the main living room. If the entry camera misses a face, the indoor camera catches movement, clothing, and direction of travel.

  • Entry camera: face-height view of arrivals and deliveries.
  • Indoor camera: wide view of the hallway or main room.
  • Skipped for now: backyard, side windows, and garage become cameras three and four later.

Why plug-in power wins when every dollar is spoken for

Plug-in cameras beat battery models on a tight budget for one mechanical reason: wall power allows continuous recording with nothing to recharge, while a battery camera rations every clip to protect its charge. Battery units suit sheds and fences with no outlet nearby, but each adds a permanent chore of recharging. Two plug-in cameras near outlets cost less to run and miss less footage.

Map your outlets before buying, walking each planned position with a phone charger. Anything beyond a cord's length from an outlet needs an extension plan routed along baseboards, never across walkways.

Record locally so there is no monthly bill to forget

Subscriptions are where tight budgets quietly die. A camera demanding a monthly plan for playback turns a one-time purchase into a recurring bill. Memory-card recording avoids that trap: each camera saves motion clips to its own card and overwrites the oldest footage when full, keeping days of recent events in your home with no account in good standing required.

One caveat: if someone steals the camera, they steal its card too. Turn on person alerts if available, narrow detection zones to walkways to cut passing-car alerts, and pull important clips to your phone the same day.

Tape it up before you drill or stick anything

Hold each camera in place with painter's tape for a full day before mounting. Check the live view morning, noon, and night, watching for backlight that turns faces into silhouettes, Wi-Fi dead spots that freeze the stream, and detection zones flooded by trees or traffic. Moving tape costs nothing; moving a drilled mount costs a wall repair.

The glare check that saves your night footage

Night footage fails more often from glare than darkness. A camera staring through a window at its own infrared reflection shows a white blob instead of a porch. Mount the lens flush against the pane, or switch off the night-vision LEDs and rely on a porch light. Five minutes of checking after sunset prevents months of useless clips.

Mount high enough to deter, low enough to recognize

A ceiling camera sees hoods and the tops of heads; a head-height camera sees faces. Aim just above reach, angled slightly down, so visitors cannot easily grab it but the lens still meets eyes. Indoors, the top of a bookshelf or an upper door frame usually lands in exactly this band.

A Saturday install order that avoids rework

  1. Morning: tape both cameras up, connect to Wi-Fi, and confirm live views and alerts from each spot.
  2. Midday: shrink motion zones to walkways and doors, then walk through to trigger a test alert.
  3. Afternoon: fix mounts, route cords along baseboards, insert memory cards, confirm recording.
  4. Evening: after dark, verify faces stay visible and glare is gone.
  5. Next morning: download one clip to prove the full chain from lens to evidence works.

Done this way, a modest budget leaves you with two reliable witnesses instead of one expensive ornament.
